B06_00: During gastrulation, cells of the early embryo leave the epithelial sheet at the primitive streak to form mesoderm, and a partial version of this transition generates definitive endoderm. Without it the germ layers cannot be laid down. The same switch is redeployed by carcinoma cells, where loss of epithelial character underlies invasion and metastasis, making this developmental step a template for tumour dissemination.
B06_01: After fertilization, the early embryo must erase the epigenetic states inherited from egg and sperm and build chromatin able to support its own gene expression. This reprogramming of both parental genomes enables activation of the embryonic genome before marks are re-established around implantation. Failure impairs preimplantation development and the handling of imprinted genes.
B06_02: During gastrulation, the lateral plate mesoderm is specified as the tissue that will build the heart, limbs, blood and the linings of the body cavity and gut. Signals from the neighbouring endoderm lock in its identity. Disturbance of this specification underlies congenital heart and diaphragm defects, and the same cues are used to derive cardiac and vascular lineages from pluripotent stem cells.
B06_03: Early in gastrulation, the midline axial mesoderm forms the prechordal plate, head process and notochord, the embryo's organising rod. It stiffens the body axis and patterns the neural tube and somites. In adults its remnants persist as the nucleus pulposus at the centre of intervertebral discs, whose degeneration underlies disc disease.
B06_04: In pigment-producing melanocytes and melanoma cells, the lineage master regulator also sets how much the cell relies on mitochondrial energy production. This matters in melanoma: high-activity tumours tend to survive targeted kinase therapy, while low-activity tumours are more invasive and drug-tolerant. It links pigment-cell identity to energetics, oxidative stress tolerance, resistance to senescence and the switching of melanoma cells between states.
B06_05: Pigment cell precursors must survive their migration from the neural crest and their colonisation of the skin during development, and mature melanocytes must persist afterwards. This survival programme makes both possible. Loss of it causes pigment cell death and depigmentation, while its persistence in melanoma supports tumour cell survival and resistance to therapy.
B06_06: In melanocytes and melanoma cells, this repressive programme decides whether a cell proliferates or switches to an invasive, drug-resistant state. When the lineage regulator falls, cells change how they attach to the surrounding matrix and acquire a migratory, mesenchymal-like character. Because high activity marks proliferative melanoma and low activity marks quiescent invasive cells, it links lineage identity to metastasis and resistance to targeted therapy.
B06_07: During pregnancy, milk-secreting alveolar cells arise in the mammary gland from luminal progenitors, as an alternative to ductal fate, and this commitment makes lactation possible. After weaning most alveolar cells are cleared during involution, but surviving precursors rebuild the secretory tissue in later pregnancies. The programme ties into the mammary stem cell hierarchy and to the origins of breast cancer subtypes.
B06_08: In the mammary gland, contractile myoepithelial cells wrap around ducts and alveoli and squeeze milk toward the nipple in response to a pituitary hormone; without them lactation fails. They also help build the basement membrane and restrain luminal outgrowth. Normally they generate only their own type, but after loss of luminal cells they can regenerate the luminal compartment.
B06_09: The anterior neural plate is the early embryonic territory that folds into the neural tube and forms the forebrain and midbrain, the first step in building a brain. Its specification sets regional identity, including the boundary between midbrain and hindbrain, as cells leave pluripotency. Failure of neural tube closure produces spina bifida and related congenital defects of the central nervous system.
B06_10: An egg enters fertilization carrying messages stored during its growth, and clearing them on schedule lets the embryo take over control of its own development. This clearance, driven by factors already stored in the oocyte and acting in the maturing egg and early zygote, is essential for fertility. When it fails, oocytes arrest, zygotes stall at early cleavage and female infertility results.
B06_11: The early embryo is initially transcriptionally silent and relies on stored maternal products; activation of its own genome is the switch that lets development continue. In humans it occurs in a minor wave at the one-cell stage and a major wave around the eight-cell stage. Without it development arrests within the first few cleavages, a cause of early embryo failure.
B06_12: Proliferating melanocytes and melanoma cells rely on their lineage master regulator to maintain genome stability, DNA replication and the ends of their chromosomes. When it is lost, damage accumulates and cells become senescent, whereas stress-driven suppression produces a reversible pause instead. This links pigment-cell identity to proliferative lifespan and to how melanoma cells switch between proliferative and invasive, dedifferentiated states.
B06_13: The luminal lineage of the mammary gland forms the inner layer of ducts and the milk-secreting alveolar cells, arising after birth from progenitors that expand during puberty and pregnancy. It builds the ductal tree and terminal ductal lobular units of the breast, linking systemic hormones to local growth. Progenitors within it are the presumed cells of origin for major breast cancer subtypes.
B06_14: During branching of the developing pancreas, undifferentiated epithelial precursors must keep proliferating until some are released to become hormone-producing islet cells. This balance determines how many beta cells form. Its disruption limits beta cell number and contributes to neonatal diabetes and pancreatic hypoplasia, conditions in which the pancreas or its endocrine compartment is underdeveloped.
B06_15: In the embryo, neural crest cells choose between becoming neurons, Schwann cells or pigment-producing melanocytes, and this regulation decides the melanocyte fate. It controls pigmentation and the migration and survival of pigment cell precursors. When deregulated it shapes melanoma behaviour, and defects in this lineage decision underlie pigmentation and hearing disorders such as Waardenburg syndrome.
B06_16: During gastrulation, cells ingressing through the anterior primitive streak become definitive endoderm, the germ layer that forms the gut tube and its organs, including liver, pancreas, thyroid and lung epithelium. This specification licenses later organ development. Directing pluripotent stem cells through this step is the starting point for making liver cells and pancreatic beta cells for regenerative medicine.
B06_17: In the vertebrate embryo, the paraxial mesoderm is periodically divided into somites, the blocks that form vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis. The size and spacing of these segments are set by a rhythmic timing system meeting positional cues. Failure produces congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis, in which vertebrae and ribs are fused or misshapen.
B06_18: The pancreas begins as buds of embryonic gut endoderm whose cells are committed to form digestive enzyme-secreting acini, ducts and hormone-producing islets, and this programme specifies and maintains that early precursor state. Much is inferred from mouse embryology, where loss causes pancreatic agenesis or hypoplasia. In humans, mutations underlie pancreatic developmental disorders, including diabetes from failed islet formation.
B06_19: Gastrulation converts the single-layered epiblast of the early embryo into three germ layers, setting out the body plan from which notochord, heart and gut all derive. It marks the shift from pluripotent cells to committed lineages. Failure of primitive streak formation arrests the embryo before any organ lineage exists.
B06_20: In the early embryo, a strip of ectoderm between the future brain and the future skin is set aside to become neural crest and cranial placodes. This territory gives vertebrates their peripheral nervous system, craniofacial skeleton, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, lens, inner ear and olfactory epithelium. Failure here underlies neurocristopathies and craniofacial malformations.
B06_21: The pancreas begins as two buds of foregut endoderm, and this lineage traces how gastrulation-stage endoderm becomes multipotent pancreatic progenitors rather than liver or bile duct cells, instructed by surrounding mesenchyme and notochord. These progenitors later form acinar, ductal and islet cells, including beta cells. Failure underlies pancreatic agenesis and neonatal diabetes, and the same cues guide stem cell-derived beta cell production.
B06_22: After fertilization the embryo must clear messages inherited from the oocyte, and this arm of the clearance is carried out by products of the embryo's own genome. Timely removal lets the embryo take control of its gene expression. When it fails, maternal transcript levels stay abnormal, development stalls and infertility follows, making it a key step of the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
B06_23: In the developing pancreas, duct-like trunk progenitors choose between ductal and endocrine fates, and this step commits them to an endocrine progenitor state that can still make all islet hormone cell types. The choice depends largely on the mechanical environment around the cells. Understanding these cues underpins efforts to direct stem cells toward beta cells for diabetes therapy.
B06_24: The skin's outer surface is continuously rebuilt as keratinocytes move upward from a basal stem cell layer through successive layers to form the cornified barrier, which blocks pathogen entry and water loss. Dead surface cells are shed and replaced throughout life. Disruption of the balance between renewal and differentiation underlies barrier-defective skin disease, impaired wound repair and keratinocyte-derived tumours.
B06_25: When hormonal and growth signals are present, cells switch off a starvation and stress programme that otherwise promotes glucose production by the liver, autophagy, growth arrest and cell death. This is how the fed state lowers hepatic glucose output and permits growth and survival. Loss of control contributes to insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia, and constant growth signalling in tumours disables this tumour-suppressive programme.
B06_26: In pigment-producing melanocytes this programme sets how mobile and invasive a cell is, influencing cell-cell adhesion and cell shape. It matters most in melanoma, where cells switch between a proliferative, differentiated state and an invasive state, so its activity helps decide whether tumour cells grow locally or metastasise and how they respond to targeted therapy. It also underlies normal pigment precursor migration.
B06_27: In melanocytes and melanoma cells, the lineage master regulator acts as a rheostat for cell division: intermediate activity drives proliferation, low activity yields slow-cycling, invasive, dedifferentiated cells, and very high activity imposes arrest. This behaviour is central to normal pigment cell biology and to melanoma, where switching between proliferative and invasive states tracks its levels independently of pigmentation.
B06_28: Mammary glands arise from embryonic surface ectoderm, and mammary stem cells derived from it found the ductal tree and can regenerate a functional gland. In the adult breast they are rare and sit in the ducts of terminal ductal lobular units. They drive bud formation, pubertal duct outgrowth and pregnancy-associated remodelling, and when misregulated contribute to stem-like compartments in breast cancer.
B06_29: Immediately after fertilization, the tightly packed sperm genome must be unpacked and rebuilt into ordinary chromatin using components supplied by the egg. This lets the paternal genome become active and take part in the first embryonic divisions, and it sets the paternal epigenome inherited by the embryo. Defects contribute to fertilization failure and infertility.
B06_30: In melanocytes and melanoma cells, the lineage master regulator also builds and acidifies the cell's degradative compartments, supporting maturation of pigment granules, receptor recycling and breakdown of cellular material. When melanoma cells are starved of nutrients, this lets them digest their own components and survive stress. It also links lipid handling to proliferation and drug resistance in melanoma.
B06_31: Circulating monocytes arise in the bone marrow, enter the blood and live only a day or two before dying or entering tissues to become macrophages and dendritic cells. They sustain innate defence: classical monocytes engulf and kill bacteria, while non-classical monocytes patrol vessels and respond to viruses. Too little leaves these compartments depleted; excess drives the inflammatory influx of atherosclerosis, autoimmunity and chronic infection.
B06_32: Nephrons are the kidney's filtering and reabsorbing units, running from the glomerulus through the tubules and loop of Henle to the collecting duct. Their formation during fetal life sets the number of nephrons a person will ever have. Defects underlie congenital kidney malformations and reduced nephron endowment, which predisposes to hypertension and chronic kidney disease later in life.
B06_33: Hormone-producing islet cells of the pancreas arise from a transient progenitor population that commits away from duct and acinar fates. Without this step no beta, alpha, delta or PP cells form. Loss-of-function mutations in humans cause congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea with permanent neonatal diabetes, and the programme is a target of efforts to make beta cells from stem cells.
B06_34: Skin, hair and eye colour depend on this pigment cell programme, which builds pigment granules in melanocytes and moves them to the cell periphery for transfer to neighbouring skin cells. Loss causes hypopigmentation and deafness syndromes, while its reactivation sustains the differentiated state of melanoma cells. It links pigmentation to developmental and stress signals acting on the skin.
B06_35: The intermediate mesoderm is the strip of embryonic mesoderm that forms the entire urogenital system, including gonads, nephric ducts, ureteric epithelium and kidney precursors. Its specification decides whether kidneys and reproductive tracts form at all. Defects underlie renal agenesis and urogenital malformations, and the same developmental cues are used to direct human pluripotent stem cells toward kidney lineages in vitro.
B06_36: The posterior neural plate forms the caudal half of the embryonic neural sheet, which gives rise to the hindbrain and anterior spinal cord. Part of it derives from progenitors that can also become paraxial mesoderm, and its specification fixes the boundary between midbrain and hindbrain. Incomplete closure of the neural tube produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida.
B06_37: The kidney and much of the male reproductive tract descend from a single embryonic tube, the nephric (Wolffian) duct, carved out of intermediate mesoderm. From its caudal end the ureteric bud emerges to build the adult kidney. This step therefore underlies formation of the urinary and male genital tracts, and failure produces renal agenesis and other congenital urinary tract anomalies.
B06_38: Pancreatic ductal cells line the branching duct tree that carries digestive secretions and alkaline fluid to the gut, and descend from early pancreatic progenitors through bipotent trunk progenitors. The surrounding connective tissue and basement membrane guide duct shape, polarity and branching. Disturbed ductal identity underlies cystic pancreatic disease and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, a cancer with dense fibrous stroma.
B06_39: The permanent kidney begins when the ureteric bud sprouts from the nephric duct into the surrounding mesenchyme, later forming the ureter and collecting ducts and inducing nephrons at its tips. Getting the number and position of buds right determines final nephron endowment. Errors produce renal agenesis, duplex or multicystic dysplastic kidneys and other congenital urinary tract anomalies.
